analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare, including dentures, glasses, and hearing aids.
analysis.headline: The bill won 121 House cosponsors but never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written dental, vision, and hearing care into Medicare itself. Today, traditional Medicare excludes almost all of this care, so seniors pay out of pocket or buy separate private coverage. The bill would have covered routine cleanings, fillings, dentures, eye exams, glasses, hearing exams, and hearing aids, with annual frequency limits and cost sharing, phasing in over several years. It never got past its first committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare, and especially lower-income seniors, who today often skip dental, vision, and hearing care because traditional Medicare does not cover it and private dental plans are thin. Roughly half of older adults have no dental coverage of any kind.

how_it_helps.text: Adds dental and oral health services to Medicare: oral exams, cleanings, x-rays, fillings, extractions, root canals, crowns, bridges, and emergency dental care [S2][S3].
Covers dentures, with a limit of one full upper and lower denture (or partial set) every five years [S3].
Adds routine eye exams and coverage of eyeglass lenses and frames up to $100 each (indexed to inflation) and contact lenses up to $200 per two years [S3].

Adds routine hearing exams and hearing aid coverage at 80 percent, limited to one hearing aid per ear every 48 months, and repeals the statutory exclusion that bars Medicare from paying for hearing aids [S3].
Gives the Health and Human Services Secretary authority to phase in, limit, or expand the new benefits, including higher payment rates for low-income subsidy-eligible beneficiaries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and Medicare, which would take on the full cost of a large new benefit; beneficiaries would also pay the standard 20 percent coinsurance on covered services.

drawbacks.text: The new benefit is expensive: adding dental, vision, and hearing to Medicare for tens of millions of beneficiaries is one of the largest possible expansions of the program, borne by federal taxpayers [S2].

Coverage is limited and phased in: Medicare would pay nothing toward basic and major dental services before 2025, eyeglass coverage is capped at $100 per lens set, hearing aids are limited to one per ear every four years, and dentures to one set every five years [S3].
Beneficiaries would owe the standard 20 percent coinsurance on these services unless the Secretary set otherwise, so out-of-pocket costs would not drop to zero [S3].
The Secretary could apply prior authorization and other limits to all the new services, leaving the eventual scope of the benefit open to future administrative decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors, especially those who skip dental and hearing care today, the benefit would be real and large. The honest cost is fiscal: this is a multibillion-dollar annual expansion of Medicare, and the caps in the bill ($100 glasses, one hearing aid per ear per four years) are modest relative to actual retail prices, so it would not have eliminated out-of-pocket costs even if enacted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, and in two years neither committee ever scheduled it for a vote; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, on the first day of the 118th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and to their health subcommittees [S5].
121 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, a majority of the Democratic caucus; no Republican cosponsored [S4].

The only action after 2023 was a second routine referral to the Health Subcommittee on December 17, 2024; no markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, Medicare Advantage insurers kept dental, vision, and hearing coverage as a selling point for their private plans, and dental, optical, and hearing aid providers kept a market where most seniors pay out of pocket or buy separate private coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare Advantage insurers and dental and hearing providers

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Dental, Vision, and Hearing Benefit Act on the first day of the 118th Congress.

for.name: 121 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members from across the Democratic caucus.

against.name: Committee leadership, House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means
against.role: Committee chairs who control whether bills get a markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in committee in January 2023 and never scheduled it for a markup or vote in two years.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Held 224 of 440 House seats and controlled the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; no Republican cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: All 121 cosponsors were House Democrats, about 56 percent of the Democratic caucus; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled House never scheduled the bill for any vote.

industries.note: Medicare payment for cleanings, fillings, crowns, and dentures would bring tens of millions of new paying patients into dental offices. Their gain is the public's gain, since untreated dental problems drive emergency room visits and broader health problems.

The bill repeals the statutory exclusion that bars Medicare from paying for hearing aids and covers them at 80 percent. Hearing aids commonly cost thousands of dollars per ear, which is why so few older adults who need them own them.
Coverage of eye exams, glasses, and contact lenses would route routine vision care through Medicare for the first time, though the $100 caps are low relative to retail prices.

Private Medicare Advantage plans currently offer dental, vision, and hearing benefits to attract enrollees away from traditional Medicare. A universal benefit under traditional Medicare would erase that advantage, so these insurers' interest in the bill ran against it, and their interest in the outcome aligned with the bill's death.

industries.industry: Standalone private dental and vision insurers
industries.note: Seniors buy separate dental and vision policies today largely because Medicare excludes this care. A Medicare benefit would shrink that market.
